extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, journalists and researchers seeking an overview of Russian laws on disinformation and media censorship
extracted.subtask_description: A descriptive summary of federal Russian legislation that defines and punishes the dissemination of 'unreliable' information (so-called 'fake news'), including major statutes from 2019, 2020 and 2022 and their effects on media. Useful as a reference for understanding the legal provisions, penalties, and practical impacts on journalists and outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on dissemination of 'unreliable' information
rubrics_metrics.description: A group of federal laws prohibiting the dissemination of information considered 'unreliable' by Russian authorities, establishing punishment for such dissemination, and allowing Roskomnadzor to extrajudicially block access to online media publishing such information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the overarching principle tying multiple statutes together; it empowers administrative and criminal sanctions and gives the Federal Service for Supervision of Communications, Information Technology and Mass Media (Roskomnadzor) authority to block access to offending online media.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2019 law No.31-FZ — blocking for 'unreliable information'
rubrics_metrics.description: Law No.31-FZ (signed 18 March 2019) allows Roskomnadzor to block access to any online media in case of revealing 'unreliable information'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gave Roskomnadzor extrajudicial power to restrict access to online outlets deemed to publish 'unreliable' information; cited as a foundational administrative enforcement tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2019 law No.27-FZ — administrative fines for publishing 'unreliable information'
rubrics_metrics.description: Law No.27-FZ (signed 18 March 2019) establishes administrative fines for natural persons and juridical persons for publication of 'unreliable information'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creates monetary penalties for individuals and organizations that publish information classified as 'unreliable' by authorities; enforcement works alongside blocking powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2019 Disrespect to Authorities Law (No.28-FZ) — punishment for online 'disrespect'
rubrics_metrics.description: Law No.28-FZ (signed 18 March 2019) punishes 'blatant disrespect online for the state, the authorities, the public, the Russian flag or the constitution' by a fine or by imprisonment for up to 15 days in the case of repeat offences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targets online expressions judged to be disrespectful; intended penalties include fines and short-term administrative imprisonment for repeat violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2019 law No.30-FZ — Roskomnadzor removal requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Law No.30-FZ (enacted 18 March 2019) allows Roskomnadzor to request the removal of statements deemed 'disrespectful' or otherwise unlawful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a mechanism for authorities to demand content removal from online platforms and media without judicial process.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2020 COVID-19 laws (No.99-FZ & No.100-FZ) — punishments for 'unreliable' epidemic information
rubrics_metrics.description: On 1 April 2020, laws No.99-FZ and No.100-FZ established administrative and criminal punishment for dissemination of unreliable information about circumstances that threaten life and health of a citizen including epidemics, natural and technological disasters, emergencies, and measures to ensure security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aimed at preventing dissemination of doubts about the nature of COVID-19 and the reasonableness of public-health measures; introduced both administrative fines and criminal liability for certain communications about epidemics and emergencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2022 'fakes' / war censorship laws (No.31‑FZ & No.32‑FZ) — criminal liability for false information about the Armed Forces
rubrics_metrics.description: On 4 March 2022 laws No.31-FZ and No.32-FZ amended the Criminal Code, adding article 207.3 'Public dissemination of knowingly false information about the use of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation', introducing criminal liability with a maximum punishment of 15 years' imprisonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically targets statements about the actions of the Russian Armed Forces; establishes severe criminal penalties for 'knowingly false' public statements regarding military operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articles 280.3 and 284.2 / Administrative articles 20.3.3 and 20.3.4 — 'discrediting' and calls for sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter 29 of the Criminal Code was supplemented by articles 280.3 (punishing 'discrediting' of the Armed Forces and its operations) and 284.2 (responsibility for calls by a Russian citizen to impose sanctions against Russia, its citizens or entities). These actions were also included in administrative Code articles 20.3.3 and 20.3.4 with graduated penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 280.3: 'discrediting' can be punished by up to five years' imprisonment. Article 284.2: calls for sanctions punishable by up to three years. Under the administrative code, a first call could incur a heavy fine, the second could lead to imprisonment; these provisions criminalize criticism and sanctions advocacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments No.62‑FZ & No.63‑FZ (25 March 2022) — expanded scope for 'discrediting' offences
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws No.62-FZ and No.63-FZ amended Article 20.3.3 of the Administrative Offenses Code and Article 280.3 of the Criminal Code to make punishable 'discrediting' of the exercise of powers by not only the Russian Armed Forces but any Russian state body (e.g., National Guard, FSB, Ministry of Emergency Situations) outside Russian territory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broadened the protected subjects and geographic scope, so criticism of many state bodies' actions abroad can trigger the same administrative or criminal sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement tools and practical effects on media
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws precipitated mass exodus and suspension of activities by foreign and independent media in Russia, forced outlets to stop covering the invasion, and led journalists to leave the country or launch operations abroad (e.g., Novaya Gazeta Europe).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates how blocking, fines, removal requests, and criminal penalties combine in practice to curtail reporting: numerous domestic independent outlets were closed or blocked and many international newsrooms suspended operations in Russia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belarus Law No.133‑Z — criminalization of appeals for sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Belarusian Law No.133-Z (14 December 2021) amended Article 361 of the Belarus Criminal Code to criminalize appeals for sanctions against Belarusian legal and natural persons, with penalties including imprisonment up to six years; appeals to foreign countries and dissemination punishable by 3–10 years, and via media/internet by 4–12 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included for comparative context: a neighboring state's law similarly criminalizes advocacy for sanctions and escalates penalties when dissemination occurs via media or the internet.
